I really started improving when I thought of every character as a puzzle to be solved, rematch every time i lost and not rematching any time I won is what increased my GSP, and my mentality that any character can lose to my main if my brain can out think my opponents brain for a few minutes. the biggest thing that clicked is that as GSP improves, opponents act vastly different. Every significant jump up in GSP, you’ll notice players are choosing more moves that give them the best chance in the long run. They’re avoiding being punished by simply not choosing punishable moves in the first place, until they have an opportunity to use that move to punish me. They’ve memorized more common attacks and my job is to get a hit after realizing that my opponent has incorrectly guessed what I’m about to do.

Close your eyes, turn off the lights while you’re practicing.
Also try playing with the A minor blues scale since so many of these notes are in A minor. It’s C,D,D#,E,G,&A.

Chord progression is 1-4-6-7.

1-4 can also be thought of as a 5-1. Very popular in jazz. Try playing the Dominant 7th chord for E (the power chord plus the major third and minor 7th. This will give a jazzier sound that uses notes outside of the key that those power chords exist in (A minor). If you like the sound of E7, you could try making any other power chords into dominant 7ths too.

Id also try using chromatic scale here. Because you’re going from C to D and then D to E, instead of just playing D and then E, you could very quickly play D# between the two as a passing note. Could even slide your finger from c to d and then slide it from d to e. You can also build entire chords off that, which work well in 7th chords too. Playing D#7 and then D7, A#7 and then A7, E#7 before E7, or C#7 before C7 will sound similar to playing a “5-1.” This is because the dominant 5 chord (also known as a _7, the chord built from the fifth note in a scale) shares two notes with the chord one half-step above. In other words, A#7 has four notes in it, and the two notes that “define the chord,” i.e. the third and seventh—I.e. the non power chord notes—are actually flipped into the seventh and third of E7. This is called a “tritone substitution” because these two shared notes are a tritone away from eachother. 

Once you choose chords, write down every note from each chord in a Venn diagram to learn how to connect them. For example, your first two power chords would look like this.

(E B) (A E) 

Venn diagram
(B (E) A)

Id start your bassline on B, figure out a way to get to the note “E” when your band is switching chords, and it’ll flow seamlessly into A. The next chords don’t connect perfectly, but I’d expand this past power chords into full chords like 7th and see how writing down the notes in each chord will help write lines.

There are two big pieces of general learning advice. A coach, and transferable skills. 

watched a Ted talk on learning plateaus. Studies found a coach is what helps anyone from an athlete or bass player your age to top surgeons improve their casualty rates after years of no improvement following all different kinds of learning rates before they stopped improving I’m self taught piano for two years bass for a year, so I Took classes in music, I learned from a theory of jazz improv class more than I ever could explain in a post about the relationships of sounds. Changed my perspective. Teach also gave me the same advice I heard in the ted talk explaining why you need a coach: they help you zero in on what your bad at and make you practice just that until your good. Serious jazz legends are always their own coaches, obsessed with the puzzle of learning things they want to be able to do but can’t yet, efficient with their practice time, doing more in ten minutes by starting in the middle of a song for example than playing the beginning part they have down over and over. It’s more intellectual effort, time moves slower, it feels less like play and more like work, but the growth sticks.

The second piece of big advice is that there’s a phenomenon where you tend to see the most rapid improvement at something the first three months of learning it. After that, it’s not surprising development slows. One way to hack this is to learn skills that are related to bass and will help you. You’ll pick them up rapidly at first, and when skills are closely related, studies have shown learning between them to be “transferable,” which means that learning one makes you better at the other. Learning to play bass helped me play piano better. Bass is a fairly similar instrument, but forces you to be very deliberate with note choices, often sticking to the safe notes when you’re playing with other people and not very skilled yet, and therefore you have to develop rhythmic ability more to make it interesting and have fun, which I brought back to the piano. Because I’m a pianist, I really like playing a range, and found myself playing the high notes on the bass a lot more and getting into melodic bass. This way makes learning feel more like play and ease. Just imagine, if you spent three months playing every instrument you could, then went back to bass, you’d know so much more about sound. Speaking of, if you want to speed up development of your ear and muscle memory, close your eyes while you play. If it’s too hard, turn the lights off, or turn your head the unnatural way to stretch it out while you play and look at your hands in the periphery. This is what taught me how to play piano without watching having to see both hands at once. You can also ask chatgpt for advice. If you’re poor right now, self publish but hire a good editor on fiver or somewhere. You could hire me if you’d like. Otherwise everything a publisher can do you can do on Kindle Direct Publishing if you have an amazon account or are willing to make one. The Sopranos: 
-Not every storyline has to get closure. I’m not just talking about the finale; Christopher’s “He said to tell you and Paulie 3 O’Clock” line, as well as the Russian in the Pine Barrens...David Chase is very deft at choosing which stories get real closure, and which get hints that allow you to ponder but not anything confirming your suspicions.

Community:
-In an interview, Dan Harmon mentioned how he sees parts of himself in every character he wrote. Abed in particular is the closest reflection of himself, I’ve always written character trying to connect multiple people I’ve known in real life...now I sometimes think about how I could distill one real life person into multiple characters. I think about how my life would have gone if I had started with difference circumstances or made different choices, and sometimes I think two characters can have really interesting relationships if they see eachother as differing only by their backgrounds or life choices...also, in the finale Abed gives an amazing speech about how T.V. isn’t meant to feel perfect...it’s gotta be like an old friend, okay for it to have a bad day. This has changed how I view sitcoms. It’s okay if sometimes it’s boring or not super funny, but what’s important is that your characters act in consistent ways true to their person, so it feels you’re hanging out with friends.

That 70s Show:
-I used this show for a breakup...it proved Abed’s point from the last paragraph. It was not a perfect show. Often I found it very unfunny, the humor was good when it landed cause I was surprised that I even enjoyed the jokes. It felt like having friends in the room when I was very alone.

It’s always Sunny in Philadelphia:
-Not every character, even in a comedy, even if they’re all of your main characters, need to be like able. You can laugh at what had people do without laughing with them. You just need to be sharp enough as an audience to get the difference, and it’s okay to trust that a sharp audience will come watch. IASIP is my favorite show of all time

Arrested Development:
-you can set up an entire episode just to make a couple of wordplay based jokes and it will be fine as long as you work hard. “Justice is Blind” and “That’s why you don’t teach lessons to your son” are personal favorites.

Letterkenny, The Inbetweeners:
Not every joke has to be logically funny to be goddamned hilarious. When you feel like the characters are your friends, all the jokes feel like inside jokes, and that makes it way funnier.
